1	# Medusa — Student Setup Guide
2	
3	This is a **course fork of [medusajs/medusa](https://github.com/medusajs/medusa)** — the open-source
4	commerce **framework monorepo** (30+ TypeScript packages). It is pinned to a verified baseline:
5	
6	- **Version:** `@medusajs/medusa` **2.17.2**
7	- **Baseline commit:** `8f97e3f371`
8	- Everyone starts from this exact commit. Do **not** pull from upstream `develop`/`main` — it moves and can break.
9	
10	📚 **Official documentation:** <https://docs.medusajs.com>
11	
12	---
13	
14	## 1. Prerequisites
15	
16	| Tool | Version | Notes |
17	| --- | --- | --- |
18	| **Node.js** | **20 LTS or 22 LTS** | Do not use Node 24 — a few test suites fail on it. Use [nvm](https://github.com/nvm-sh/nvm). |
19	| **Corepack** | ships with Node | Run `corepack enable` — it activates the repo-pinned **Yarn 3.2.1** automatically. Do not install Yarn globally. |
20	| **Docker** | any recent | Only needed for **integration tests** (and for running a real store DB). |
21	| **Git** | any | |
22	
23	> 💡 **New to Turborepo or Yarn workspaces?** This monorepo holds 30+ TypeScript packages built with [Turborepo](https://turbo.build/repo/docs). The key things to know: always run commands from the repo root; use `yarn workspace @medusajs/<name> <command>` to target one package; and run `yarn build` after install — packages depend on each other's build output.
24	
25	> 📖 **Architecture overview:** [docs.medusajs.com/learn](https://docs.medusajs.com/learn) explains the module system, commerce modules, and how the packages fit together. Read the *Framework* section before exploring the source.
26	
27	**OS:** Linux, macOS, or **Windows via WSL2** recommended.
28	
29	---
30	
31	## 2. First-time setup
32	
33	```bash
34	git clone <your-team-fork-url>
35	cd medusa
36	corepack enable          # activates Yarn 3.2.1 from the repo
37	yarn install             # ~1-2 min
38	yarn build               # ~4 min — builds all 80 packages; REQUIRED before running tests
39	```
40	
41	`yarn install` prints ~19 warnings (native-module "must be built" notices + one TS compat-patch
42	line) — these are **benign**. `yarn build` should end with `80 successful, 80 total`.
43	
44	---
45	
46	## 3. Start the project
47	
48	```bash
49	# Admin dashboard dev server (Vite):
50	yarn workspace @medusajs/dashboard dev
51	
52	# Design-system component explorer (Storybook, http://localhost:6006):
53	yarn workspace @medusajs/ui storybook
54	
55	# Full store + admin with seed data (needs the Postgres from step 5):
56	npx create-medusa-app@latest my-store \
57	  --db-url "postgres://postgres:postgres@localhost:5433/my_store"
58	cd my-store && yarn dev        # admin at http://localhost:9000/app
59	```
60	
61	---
62	
63	## 4. Testing — backend (Jest) & frontend (Vitest)
64	
65	```bash
66	# FULL unit baseline across all packages. KEEP --continue:
67	# plain `yarn test` aborts on the first failing package and won't run the rest.
68	yarn turbo run test --no-daemon --no-cache --force --continue
69	
70	# A single package:
71	yarn workspace @medusajs/order test        # backend (Jest)
72	yarn workspace @medusajs/dashboard test    # frontend (Vitest)
73	yarn workspace @medusajs/ui test           # frontend (Vitest)
74	
75	# A single file:
76	yarn jest <path/to/file.spec.ts>
77	```
78	
79	---
80	
81	## 5. Testing — integration (needs Docker)
82	
83	Start a Postgres (and Redis, only for the `*-redis` modules) on non-default host ports:
84	
85	```bash

87	docker run -d --name medusa-redis -p 6380:6379 redis:7-alpine
88	```

90	Run integration tests with the DB env vars (the runner creates throwaway temp DBs):

_**Agent (claude-sonnet-5 2026-09-12 21:11:52Z)**_

Found it. There's a real React version conflict causing this — and a second issue (a stale server squatting on the port). Let me explain both before touching anything.

**Root cause of the CJS/ESM error:** `create-medusa-app`'s combined backend+storefront scaffold puts everything in one npm workspace. The Next.js storefront needs React 19, but the Medusa backend/admin dashboard needs React 18. npm hoists React 19.0.5 to the workspace root, and only partially nests React 18.3.1 (under `@medusajs/dashboard` and the backend package itself) — but sibling packages the dashboard actually renders with at runtime (`react-router-dom`, `react-i18next`, `@tanstack/react-query`) have **no nested React**, so they resolve up to the hoisted **React 19** copy. The admin UI ends up running React 18 and React 19 side by side, which is exactly what throws the "does not provide an export named 'default'" CJS/ESM error and blanks the page.

I verified this identically in two separate `my-store` installs:
- `~/my-store` (home directory) — **this is the one currently running** and squatting on port 9000 (PID 41721, started via `medusa start`, not `dev`)
- `medusa/my-store` (inside this repo, untracked) — same conflict, not currently running

Since there are two separate installs, I want to confirm which one is your actual project before I stop a running process and change dependency files.

1	# AGENTS.md
2	
3	## Overview
4	
5	Medusa DTC Starter — a Turborepo workspace monorepo containing a Medusa backend (`@medusajs/medusa` latest, Node 20+, PostgreSQL 15+) and an optional storefront (Next.js, Tanstack, etc...).
6	
7	## Directory Structure
8	
9	```text
10	.
11	├── apps/
12	│   ├── backend/                  # Medusa application (@dtc/backend)
13	│   │   ├── medusa-config.ts      # Medusa config: DB URL, CORS, secrets, modules
14	│   │   ├── integration-tests/    # setup.js (Jest setupFiles) and http/*.spec.ts suites
15	│   │   └── src/
16	│   │       ├── admin/            # Admin dashboard extensions (widgets/, i18n/, routes)
17	│   │       ├── api/              # API routes: api/store/*, api/admin/* (file-based)
18	│   │       ├── jobs/             # Scheduled jobs
19	│   │       ├── links/            # Module links between modules
20	│   │       ├── migration-scripts/# Data migration scripts (e.g. initial-data-seed.ts)
21	│   │       ├── modules/          # Custom modules (service + models + migrations)
22	│   │       ├── subscribers/      # Event subscribers
23	│   │       └── workflows/        # Workflows and workflow steps
24	│   └── storefront/               # OPTIONAL storefront
25	├── eslint.config.ts              # Root ESLint: @medusajs/eslint-plugin recommended
26	├── turbo.json                    # Task graph: build, dev, start, lint, test, seed
27	```
28	
29	**`apps/storefront` is optional and may not exist.** It is skipped when the user chooses not to install it. Before running any storefront command, referencing storefront files, or assuming a full-stack change is possible, check that `apps/storefront/` exists. If it doesn't, the project is backend-only — do not scaffold it or suggest it was deleted by mistake.
30	
31	Each app can have its own nested `AGENTS.md`; agents read the nearest one in the directory tree, so put app-specific context there rather than expanding this file.
32	
33	## Package Manager
34	
35	**The package manager is chosen at install time and is not fixed.** Detect it before running anything, in this order:
36	
37	1. The `packageManager` field in the root `package.json` (e.g. `"pnpm@10.11.1"`) — authoritative when present.
38	2. The lockfile at the repo root: `pnpm-lock.yaml` → pnpm, `yarn.lock` → yarn, `package-lock.json` → npm.
39	
40	```bash
41	node -p "require('./package.json').packageManager ?? 'unset'"
42	ls pnpm-lock.yaml yarn.lock package-lock.json bun.lock bun.lockb 2>/dev/null
43	```
44	
45	Use that manager for every command and never introduce a second lockfile. Below, `<pm>` means the detected manager. The `<pm> run <script>` and `<pm> exec <bin>` forms work across npm, pnpm, yarn, and bun; workspace-filter flags do not, so the per-app commands below `cd` into the app instead.
46	
47	## Commands
48	
49	Run from the repo root unless noted. Turbo skips missing apps automatically.
50	
51	### Development
52	
53	```bash
54	<pm> run dev                # all apps
55	<pm> run backend:dev        # backend only (http://localhost:9000, admin at /app)
56	<pm> run storefront:dev     # storefront only (http://localhost:8000)
57	```
58	
59	### Build
60	
61	```bash
62	<pm> run build              # all apps
63	<pm> run start              # build (via turbo dependsOn) then start
64	```
65	
66	### Lint
67	
68	```bash
69	<pm> run lint                          # all apps via turbo
70	cd apps/backend && <pm> run lint       # medusa lint
71	cd apps/storefront && <pm> run lint    # next lint
72	```
73	
74	### Test (backend only; the storefront has no test suite)
75	
76	```bash
77	<pm> run test                                              # all test tasks via turbo
78	cd apps/backend && <pm> run test:unit                      # **/src/**/__tests__/**/*.unit.spec.ts
79	cd apps/backend && <pm> run test:integration:modules       # **/src/modules/*/__tests__/**
80	cd apps/backend && <pm> run test:integration:http          # **/integration-tests/http/*.spec.ts
81	```
82	
83	Single test — pass a path/pattern through to Jest, keeping `TEST_TYPE`:
84	
85	```bash
86	cd apps/backend && <pm> run test:unit -- src/modules/foo/__tests__/service.unit.spec.ts
87	cd apps/backend && <pm> run test:unit -- -t "returns the cart"
88	```
89	
90	### Database
91	
92	```bash
93	cd apps/backend
94	<pm> exec medusa db:generate <module-name>   # generate migrations for a custom module
95	<pm> exec medusa db:migrate                  # run migrations
96	<pm> exec medusa user -e admin@test.com -p supersecret
97	<pm> run backend:seed                        # from root; seeds initial data
98	```
99	
100	## Medusa Skills & MCP Server
101	
102	These are optional but strongly recommended — they give documentation-backed answers instead of guesses about Medusa APIs. **Use them when available; if they are not, mention to the user that installing them meaningfully improves development on this project.**
103	
104	**Agentic skills** ([docs](https://docs.medusajs.com/learn/introduction/build-with-llms-ai/agentic-skills)) — if the `medusa-dev` skills are listed as available, load them *before* writing code, not after:
105	
106	- `building-with-medusa` — any backend work: modules, API routes, workflows, data models, module links
107	- `building-admin-dashboard-customizations` — anything under `apps/backend/src/admin`
108	- `building-storefronts` — anything under `apps/storefront`
109	- `db-generate` / `db-migrate` / `new-user` — the DB and user commands above
110	
111	If they are not installed, suggest:
112	
113	```bash
114	/plugin marketplace add medusajs/medusa-agent-skills
115	/plugin install medusa-dev@medusa
116	```
117	
118	**MCP server** ([docs](https://docs.medusajs.com/learn/introduction/build-with-llms-ai/mcp-server)) — a `medusa` MCP server exposing the official docs. Prefer it over web search or memory for any Medusa API, config, or upgrade question. If it is not connected, suggest:
119	
120	```bash
121	claude mcp add --transport http medusa https://docs.medusajs.com/mcp # or agent equivalent
122	```
123	
124	## Code Style
125	
126	- **The backend must satisfy `@medusajs/eslint-plugin`'s recommended config** (`eslint.config.ts`). Its rules encode Medusa framework requirements — correct route/workflow/module shapes, not just cosmetics — so a lint failure usually means the code is actually wrong, not just badly formatted. Never disable a `@medusajs/*` rule to make lint pass; fix the code.
127	- No semicolons. Double quotes, 2-space indent.
128	- Files: kebab-case. Types/classes: PascalCase. Functions/variables: camelCase. DB columns: snake_case.
129	- No emojis in code, comments, or commit messages.
130	
131	## Conventions
132	
133	- **Backend routing is file-based.** A store endpoint is `src/api/store/<path>/route.ts` exporting `GET`/`POST`/etc. Don't add a router or register routes manually.
134	- **Business logic belongs in workflows**, not in route handlers. Routes resolve and run a workflow; workflows compose steps.
135	- Adding a task to `turbo.json` requires declaring its `outputs`, or Turbo will cache nothing/the wrong thing.
136	
137	## Common Mistakes
138	
139	- Running storefront commands without checking that `apps/storefront/` exists.
140	- Assuming a package manager instead of detecting it, or running a command that creates a second lockfile.
141	- Installing a dependency at the root instead of inside the app that needs it (`cd apps/backend && <pm> add <pkg>`).
142	- Editing a custom module's model without running `<pm> exec medusa db:generate <module>` — the migration is missing and the change silently never applies.
143	- Writing raw SQL or importing DB clients directly in the backend instead of going through module services / workflows.
144	- Calling the Medusa API from the storefront without `NEXT_PUBLIC_MEDUSA_PUBLISHABLE_KEY`; requests fail with a publishable-key error, not an obvious 401.
145	- Running the test task without a reachable PostgreSQL — integration suites need a live DB.
146	- Silencing `@medusajs/*` ESLint rules instead of fixing the underlying pattern.
147	
148	## Off-Limits
149	
150	- `apps/backend/.medusa/`, `.next/`, `dist/`, `out/`, `.turbo/` — build output, excluded from the workspace and regenerated.
151	- The lockfile (`pnpm-lock.yaml`, `yarn.lock`, `package-lock.json` — whichever this install produced) — never hand-edit or delete; change it only as a side effect of a package manager command.
152	- `.env` / `.env.local` — never commit, print, or copy secret values out of them. Edit `.env.template` instead when documenting a new variable.
153	- Existing migrations in `src/modules/*/migrations/` — add a new migration rather than rewriting one that may already have run.
154	- Don't run destructive DB commands (drops, `db:migrate --help`-style flags that reset state) against the user's database without explicit confirmation.
155
```

_**Agent (claude-sonnet-5 2026-09-12 21:20:25Z)**_

Fixed. Two separate problems were causing this:

**1. Root cause of the blank screen / CJS-ESM error:** `create-medusa-app`'s combined backend+storefront scaffold puts both apps in one npm workspace. The Next.js storefront needs React 19; the Medusa backend/admin dashboard needs React 18. npm hoists React 19 to the workspace root, but only *some* admin-runtime packages (`@medusajs/dashboard` itself) get a nested React 18 copy — others the dashboard depends on at runtime (`react-router-dom`, `react-i18next`, `@tanstack/react-query`) had no nested copy and were resolving up to the hoisted **React 19**. Two React majors loaded into the same page is exactly what throws the "does not provide an export named 'default'" error and blanks `/app`.

Fix: added the officially-supported `admin.vite` hook in `medusa-config.ts` to force Vite to dedupe React:
```ts
admin: {
  vite: (config) => {
    config.resolve = config.resolve || {}
    config.resolve.dedupe = [...(config.resolve.dedupe || []), "react", "react-dom"]
    return config
  },
},
```
I verified this in both installs — Vite's `optimizeDeps` metadata now shows `react-router-dom`'s bundle importing the same underlying React chunk as the dashboard's own React import, i.e., a single deduped instance (previously they'd have pulled from different physical copies).

Applied to:
- [my-store/apps/backend/medusa-config.ts](my-store/apps/backend/medusa-config.ts) (repo-local)

_**User (2026-09-12 21:28:15Z)**_

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page - what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is not part of this read: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it - a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first - CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world - its materials, instruments, vernacular - is where distinctive choices come from. Whatever the treatment, carry at least one detail only this subject would have - its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art - as content, not ornament; it costs a plain page nothing. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits - link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Load libraries, don't paste them.** When the page genuinely needs a library - React, a charting or highlighting package - load its UMD build from cdnjs (only the script - a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined) with one pinned `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` placed before the inline script that uses its global, instead of inlining the library's source or hand-writing a stand-in; the Artifact tool's description lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images and its data ship with the page. Most pages need no library at all - reach for one only when it carries real weight.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject - the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* - most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token - a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it - a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first - don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme - then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width - set once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, whose vertical padding uses `padding-block`, never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides - and let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (~400px). Images and any `aspect-ratio` box get `max-width: 100%`, and nothing gets a `min-width` wider than the screen; only wide tables, code and diagrams may run past it - each gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Compose repeated things as one object.** Cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, badges on siblings: same edges, baselines and inner padding from one to the next, and a recurring element sits in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over dead space or sits alone in a row. Text that can outgrow its track wraps or scrolls in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Not everything is a card.** Border, fill, radius and shadow each say "separate object" - spend them by role, lifting the one thing that needs it, instead of one radius and one shadow stamped on every block, which flattens the hierarchy. Lead with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to the scale.** One scale places marks, ticks and labels, and every label names a value the chart reaches; chart text takes its color from the theme tokens so it reads in both themes; marks, labels and edges stay clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds - in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Show the page at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, without scrolling to trigger it - that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all get. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never parked at `opacity: 0` waiting on an observer. Size a hero to what it holds, not to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the page itself out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state - the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, a form someone plausibly filled, plainly marked as examples and never passed off as the user's own figures - so the first look shows what it does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly - their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give every form control a stable `id` (the platform carries form values, focus and scroll across a republish). For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out - a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen - name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it - no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject - or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name - a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word - a greeting, a category, a page-type label - the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number - a pill, a chip, a severity stripe - so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Start with what the viewer should be able to do on the page, not only what they will read: if it should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user; a page that is only read needs none of that.

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan - a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4-6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles - a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

**Write, look once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once - one screenshot of the local file, or the Artifact tool's preview where it offers one - then one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look. For a page that charts real numbers, take that look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. Don't build a test loop around your own file: no repeated screenshots, no pulling the script out to run it through node, no scripts that probe the DOM. That loop spends the session re-checking what a careful write already settled, while the user waits for a link. Then publish, check once any `window.claude` call the preview couldn't run, and stop: the live page is the review surface, and further polish is the user's to ask for. If the user reports something visibly broken - a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing - fix that and republish once.

**Open viewers** You don't need to do anything for viewers who already have the page open - published changes reach them automatically at their next quiet moment, with state carried where possible. If your page holds state a viewer would miss (a game, a long form), register `window.claude?.hot?.snapshot(...)` and boot through `window.claude?.hot?.ready ? window.claude.hot.ready(start) : start(window.claude?.hot?.data ?? {})`.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world - headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

  <div class="eyebrow">Incident summary — CSCI 535 course project</div>
  <h1>Admin dashboard blank screen at localhost:9000/app</h1>

  <div class="meta">
    <div class="meta-item">
      <span class="meta-label">Status</span>
      <span class="badge">Resolved</span>
    </div>
    <div class="meta-item">
      <span class="meta-label">Component</span>
      <span class="meta-value">@medusajs/dashboard (Vite admin build)</span>
    </div>
    <div class="meta-item">
      <span class="meta-label">Installs affected</span>
      <span class="meta-value">2 of 2 (both my-store installs)</span>
    </div>
    <div class="meta-item">
      <span class="meta-label">Date</span>
      <span class="meta-value">2026-09-12</span>
    </div>
  </div>

  <section>
    <h2>Summary</h2>
    <div class="summary">
      <p>The Medusa admin UI loaded a blank page and threw a React CJS/ESM export error in the console. Two unrelated problems were compounding: a leftover server process still bound to port 9000 from an earlier run, and a genuine dependency conflict — the project's Next.js storefront and its Medusa backend require different major versions of React, and npm's default hoisting left part of the admin bundle pointed at the wrong one. The fix pins the admin build to a single React instance using Vite's <code>dedupe</code> option, exposed by Medusa's own <code>admin.vite</code> config hook.</p>
    </div>
  </section>

  <section>
    <h2>Symptom</h2>
    <p><code>GET /app</code> returned <code>200</code> and rendered an empty <code>&lt;div id="medusa"&gt;</code> — no visible UI. The browser console reported a module error of the shape <em>"does not provide an export named 'default'"</em>, the signature of two incompatible copies of React being loaded into one page.</p>
  </section>

  <section>
    <h2>Investigation</h2>
    <ol class="steps">
      <li><p>Confirmed a server was already bound to port 9000, left running by Medusa's dev-mode file-watcher, which supervises and restarts its own server child independently of the parent <code>npm run dev</code> process.</p></li>
      <li><p>Mapped the workspace layout: <code>create-medusa-app</code> scaffolds one npm workspace holding both the Medusa backend (<code>apps/backend</code>, React 18.3.1) and a Next.js storefront (<code>apps/storefront</code>, React 19.0.5).</p></li>
      <li><p>Traced how npm actually resolved <code>react</code> across that tree: it hoisted <code>react@19.0.5</code> to the workspace root, and nested a private <code>react@18.3.1</code> only under <code>@medusajs/dashboard</code> and the backend's own <code>node_modules</code>.</p></li>
      <li><p>Checked the packages the dashboard renders with at runtime — <code>react-router-dom</code>, <code>react-i18next</code>, <code>@tanstack/react-query</code> — and found none had a nested React copy, so their imports resolved up to the hoisted <strong>React 19</strong>.</p></li>
      <li><p>Net effect: the dashboard's own components ran on React 18 while its router, i18n layer, and data-fetching hooks ran on React 19, in the same page — two incompatible instances, matching the console error and the blank render.</p></li>
    </ol>
  </section>

  <section>
    <h2>Root cause</h2>
    <p>An unresolved React major-version split (18 vs. 19) between two apps sharing one npm workspace, compounded by npm's hoisting only partially nesting the older version the backend needed.</p>

    <div class="diagram-grid">
      <div class="diagram">
        <div class="diagram-head bad">Before — split instances</div>
        <pre><span class="tok-dim">apps/backend</span> <span class="tok-dim">(needs react@18)</span>
├─ node_modules/<span class="tok-good">react@18.3.1</span>
│    <span class="tok-dim">used by @dtc/backend,</span>
│    <span class="tok-dim">@medusajs/dashboard</span>
│
└─ react-router-dom ─┐
   react-i18next      ├─→ <span class="tok-bad">react@19.0.5</span>
   @tanstack/react-   ┘   <span class="tok-dim">(hoisted root copy —</span>
   query                  <span class="tok-dim">wrong major version)</span></pre>
      </div>
      <div class="diagram">
        <div class="diagram-head good">After — one instance</div>
        <pre><span class="tok-dim">Vite (admin build)</span>
resolve.dedupe:
  [<span class="tok-accent">"react"</span>, <span class="tok-accent">"react-dom"</span>]

<span class="tok-dim">→ every import of react/</span>
<span class="tok-dim">  react-dom, regardless</span>
<span class="tok-dim">  of which package asks,</span>
<span class="tok-dim">  resolves to the same</span>
  <span class="tok-good">react@18.3.1</span> <span class="tok-dim">module</span></pre>
      </div>
    </div>
  </section>

  <section>
    <h2>Fix applied</h2>
    <p>Added Medusa's officially supported <code>admin.vite</code> hook in <code>medusa-config.ts</code>, rather than restructuring the npm workspace or pinning a React version globally — a global pin would have forced the storefront onto React 18, an unrelated regression.</p>
    <div class="codeblock">
      <div class="codeblock-head">apps/backend/medusa-config.ts</div>
      <pre><span class="kw">admin</span>: {
  <span class="kw">vite</span>: (config) => {
    config.resolve = config.resolve || {}
    config.resolve.dedupe = [
      ...(config.resolve.dedupe || []),
      <span class="str">"react"</span>,
      <span class="str">"react-dom"</span>,
    ]
    <span class="kw">return</span> config
  },
},</pre>
    </div>
  </section>

  <section>
    <h2>Verification</h2>
    <ul class="evidence">
      <li>Vite's dependency pre-bundle metadata (<code>node_modules/.vite/deps/_metadata.json</code>) now shows <code>react</code> and <code>react-dom</code> resolving from a single source path.</li>
      <li><code>react-router-dom</code>'s pre-bundled module imports the same underlying chunk file as the dashboard's own React import — one shared instance instead of two.</li>
      <li>Restarted the backend and confirmed <code>http://localhost:9000/app</code> responds <code>200</code> with no errors in the server log.</li>
      <li>Repeated the same fix and checks in a second, independent install of the same starter, to confirm the diagnosis generalizes rather than being specific to one install.</li>
    </ul>
  </section>

  <section>
    <h2>Secondary issue: stale port</h2>
    <div class="note"><strong>Operational note —</strong> Medusa's dev-mode file-watcher supervises and restarts its own server process independently of the npm process tree. Terminating the <code>npm run dev</code> process alone does not free the port: the supervised child process has to be stopped as well, or it keeps listening on 9000 across sessions.</div>
  </section>

  <section>
    <h2>Files changed</h2>
    <div class="filelist">
      <div class="fileitem"><b>medusa-config.ts</b> — repo-local <code>my-store/apps/backend/</code>: added the <code>admin.vite</code> dedupe hook</div>
      <div class="fileitem"><b>medusa-config.ts</b> — home-directory <code>~/my-store/apps/backend/</code>: same fix, applied to the second install</div>
    </div>
  </section>

  <footer>
    <span class="eyebrow">Medusa 2.17.2 course fork · admin dashboard</span>
    <span class="badge">Resolved</span>
  </footer>
</div>

12	export function createOrderTableAdapter(): TableAdapter<HttpTypes.AdminOrder> {
13	  return createTableAdapter<HttpTypes.AdminOrder>({
14	    entity: "orders",
15	    queryPrefix: "o",
16	    pageSize: 20,
17	    transformColumns: (columns) => {
18	      const ALLOWED_FILTER_FIELDS = [
19	        "id",
20	        "status",
21	        "sales_channel.id",
22	        "region.id",
23	        "customer.id",
24	        "created_at",
25	        "updated_at",
26	        "total",
27	      ]
28	
29	      const DISABLED_SORTING_PATTERNS = [
30	        /total/i,
31	        /payment_status/,
32	        /fulfillment_status/,
33	        /customer.id/,
34	        /region.id/,
35	        /sales_channel.id/,
36	      ]
37	
38	      return columns.map((column) => {
39	        const isFilterDisabled = !ALLOWED_FILTER_FIELDS.includes(column.field)
40	
41	        const isSortingDisabled = DISABLED_SORTING_PATTERNS.some((pattern) =>
42	          pattern.test(column.field)
43	        )
44	
45	        return {
46	          ...column,
47	          filter: isFilterDisabled
48	            ? { ...column.filter, enabled: false }
49	            : column.filter,
50	          sortable: isSortingDisabled ? false : column.sortable,
51	        }
52	      })
53	    },
54	    useData: (fields, params) => {
55	      const { orders, count, isError, error, isLoading } = useOrders(
56	        {
57	          fields,
58	          ...params,
59	        },
60	        {
61	          placeholderData: (previousData, previousQuery) => {
62	            // Only keep placeholder data if the fields haven't changed
63	            const prevFields =
64	              // @ts-ignore not sure what the expected type here is
65	              previousQuery?.[previousQuery?.length - 1]?.query?.fields
66	            if (prevFields && prevFields !== fields) {
67	              // Fields changed, don't use placeholder data
68	              return undefined
69	            }
70	            // Fields are the same, keep previous data for smooth transitions
71	            return previousData
72	          },
73	        }
74	      )
75	
76	      return {
77	        data: orders,
78	        count,
79	        isLoading,
80	        isError,
81	        error,
82	      }
83	    },
84	
85	    getRowHref: (row) => `/orders/${row.id}`,
86	
87	    emptyState: {
88	      empty: {
89	        heading: "No orders found",
90	      },
91	    },
92	  })
93	}

29

31	      const align = adapter?.getColumnAlignment?.(apiColumn) ?? renderer.align
32	
33	      const accessor = (row: TData) => getColumnValue(row, apiColumn)
34

582	export function getCellRenderer(
583	  renderType?: string,
584	  dataType?: string
585	): CellRendererDefinition {
586	  const definition = renderType ? cellRenderers.get(renderType) : undefined
587	  if (definition) {
588	    return definition
589	  }
590	
591	  switch (dataType) {
592	    case "date":
593	      return { render: DateRenderer }
594	    case "boolean":
595	      return { render: BooleanRenderer, align: "center" }
596	    case "enum":
597	      return { render: StatusRenderer, align: "center" }
598	    case "currency":
599	      return { render: CurrencyRenderer, align: "right" }

  cell: ({ getValue }) => {

}),

I found no importer of this hook either — it is not referenced by `order-list-table.tsx`, `configurable-order-list-table.tsx`, or `order-table-adapter.tsx`.

Here's where this fits in the dashboard's architecture, based on tracing the actual render path (no files touched).

## How the payment status badge is rendered today

There are **two live code paths**, gated by the `view_configurations` feature flag in [order-list.tsx](packages/admin/dashboard/src/routes/orders/order-list/order-list.tsx#L9-L30):

**Path A — default table (flag off):**
[`PaymentStatusCell`](packages/admin/dashboard/src/components/table/table-cells/order/payment-status-cell/payment-status-cell.tsx) is wired in via [use-order-table-columns.tsx:83-90](packages/admin/dashboard/src/hooks/table/columns/use-order-table-columns.tsx#L83-L90). It resolves the label/color with `getOrderPaymentStatus` ([order-helpers.ts:14-41](packages/admin/dashboard/src/lib/order-helpers.ts#L14-L41)) and hands off rendering to the shared, **deprecated** [`StatusCell`](packages/admin/dashboard/src/components/table/table-cells/common/status-cell/status-cell.tsx#L1-L35) — the component that actually draws the colored dot + `<span className="truncate">{children}</span>`. `StatusCell` is generic (color-in, children-out), so it's also used by `FulfillmentStatusCell` and any other status badge, not just payment.

**Path B — configurable table (flag on):**
`ConfigurableDataTable` dispatches by column type through [`getCellRenderer`](packages/admin/dashboard/src/lib/table/cell-renderers.tsx#L582-L599), which for `payment_status` resolves to `StatusRenderer` ([cell-renderers.tsx:101-122](packages/admin/dashboard/src/lib/table/cell-renderers.tsx#L101-L122)). This path renders `@medusajs/ui`'s `StatusBadge` **directly**, bypassing `StatusCell` entirely.

This matters: **a fix in `StatusCell` alone won't cover Path B.** Whichever path is actually active in this install needs to be checked, and if both are meant to stay live, both need the change.

(There are also two unused/dead duplicate column-definition hooks — `use-order-data-table-columns.tsx` in both `hooks/table/columns/` and the route-local `order-list/components/order-list-table/hooks/` — that define their own inline payment-status cells but aren't imported anywhere. Not worth touching; flagging so they aren't mistaken for the live implementation.)

## Where the change belongs

**`StatusCell`** ([status-cell.tsx](packages/admin/dashboard/src/components/table/table-cells/common/status-cell/status-cell.tsx)) is the right place for Path A, because it's the shared primitive every status badge (payment, fulfillment, etc.) already funnels through — fixing it here fixes truncation for the whole family of status columns, not just payment, with one change. The alternative — patching `PaymentStatusCell` only — would fix payment status but leave fulfillment status with the same bug, duplicating the same tooltip logic per status type.

For Path B, the equivalent fix belongs in `StatusRenderer` inside [cell-renderers.tsx](packages/admin/dashboard/src/lib/table/cell-renderers.tsx#L101-L122), since it renders `StatusBadge` independently of `StatusCell`.

There's also a newer, non-deprecated sibling, [`DataTableStatusCell`](packages/admin/dashboard/src/components/data-table/components/data-table-status-cell/data-table-status-cell.tsx), structurally identical to `StatusCell` but marked as its intended replacement. It has the same missing-tooltip gap and should get the same fix for consistency, even if nothing currently imports it for payment status — otherwise the bug reappears the moment code migrates off the deprecated component.

## The pattern already established in this codebase

The dashboard already has a house pattern for exactly this problem — conditionally-shown tooltips on truncated table-cell text — so this isn't a new interaction to design, just one to apply to status cells:

- [`ConditionalTooltip`](packages/admin/dashboard/src/components/common/conditional-tooltip/conditional-tooltip.tsx#L1-L20) wraps `@medusajs/ui`'s `Tooltip` (a Radix-based component, [exported from the design system](packages/design-system/ui/src/components/tooltip/tooltip.tsx)) and only renders it when a `showTooltip` boolean is true — otherwise it renders the children unwrapped.
- [`TextCell`](packages/admin/dashboard/src/components/table/table-cells/common/text-cell/text-cell.tsx#L1-L46) is the reference consumer: it wraps its truncated `<span>` in `ConditionalTooltip`, passing `content={text}` and `showTooltip={stringLength > 20}`.

Applying the same shape to `StatusCell` means wrapping its existing `<span className="truncate">{children}</span>` in `ConditionalTooltip`, with `content={children}` and a `showTooltip` condition based on the label length (or, more robustly, an actual overflow check via `scrollWidth > clientWidth` on a ref, which would trigger only when the column is genuinely too narrow rather than by a fixed character count — the `TextCell` precedent uses the simpler length heuristic, so matching it keeps the codebase consistent, but it's worth deciding which tradeoff you want).

No new dependency is needed — `@medusajs/ui`'s `Tooltip` is already a project dependency and already used in over a hundred places in the dashboard, including other table cells like [`country-cell.tsx`](packages/admin/dashboard/src/components/table/table-cells/order/country-cell/country-cell.tsx#L17-L29).

1	import React, { createContext, useContext } from "react"
2	import { useFeatureFlags, FeatureFlags } from "../../hooks/api/feature-flags"
3	
4	interface FeatureFlagContextValue {
5	  flags: FeatureFlags
6	  isLoading: boolean
7	  isFeatureEnabled: (flag: keyof FeatureFlags) => boolean
8	}
9	
10	const FeatureFlagContext = createContext<FeatureFlagContextValue | null>(null)
11	
12	export const useFeatureFlag = (flag: keyof FeatureFlags): boolean => {
13	  const context = useContext(FeatureFlagContext)
14	  if (!context) {
15	    // If no context, assume feature is disabled
16	    return false
17	  }
18	  return context.isFeatureEnabled(flag)
19	}
20	
21	export const useFeatureFlagContext = () => {
22	  const context = useContext(FeatureFlagContext)
23	  if (!context) {
24	    throw new Error(
25	      "useFeatureFlagContext must be used within FeatureFlagProvider"
26	    )
27	  }
28	  return context
29	}
30	
31	interface FeatureFlagProviderProps {
32	  children: React.ReactNode
33	}
34	
35	export const FeatureFlagProvider: React.FC<FeatureFlagProviderProps> = ({
36	  children,
37	}) => {
38	  const { data: flags = {}, isLoading } = useFeatureFlags()
39	
40	  const isFeatureEnabled = (flag: keyof FeatureFlags): boolean => {
41	    const enabled = flags[flag] === true
42	    return enabled
43	  }
44	
45	  return (
46	    <FeatureFlagContext.Provider value={{ flags, isLoading, isFeatureEnabled }}>
47	      {children}
48	    </FeatureFlagContext.Provider>
49	  )
50	}
51

## 1. `view_configurations` feature flag

**Definition of the flag shape** — `packages/admin/dashboard/src/hooks/api/feature-flags.tsx:4-9`:
```ts
export type FeatureFlags = {
  view_configurations?: boolean
  translation?: boolean
  rbac?: boolean
  [key: string]: boolean | undefined
}
```
This same file's `useFeatureFlags()` hook (lines 11-27) fetches the value from the backend via `sdk.client.fetch("/admin/feature-flags")` (a React Query hook, `queryKey: ["admin", "feature-flags"]`). There is no local default of `true` anywhere in the dashboard — the value is whatever the server returns for `feature_flags.view_configurations`.

**Where it's read/evaluated** — `packages/admin/dashboard/src/providers/feature-flag-provider/index.tsx`:
```ts
export const useFeatureFlag = (flag: keyof FeatureFlags): boolean => {
  const context = useContext(FeatureFlagContext)
  if (!context) {
    // If no context, assume feature is disabled
    return false
  }
  return context.isFeatureEnabled(flag)
}
...
export const FeatureFlagProvider: React.FC<FeatureFlagProviderProps> = ({ children }) => {
  const { data: flags = {}, isLoading } = useFeatureFlags()

  const isFeatureEnabled = (flag: keyof FeatureFlags): boolean => {
    const enabled = flags[flag] === true
    return enabled
  }
  ...
}
```
Key points, with exact line refs:
- `index.tsx:38` — `flags` defaults to `{}` if the query hasn't resolved/errored.
- `index.tsx:40-43` — `isFeatureEnabled` strictly checks `flags[flag] === true`; any falsy/missing/undefined value (including while loading, i.e. `{}`) evaluates to `false`.
- `index.tsx:12-19` — outside of a `FeatureFlagProvider` context, `useFeatureFlag` also defaults to `false`.

Consumers calling `useFeatureFlag("view_configurations")`:
- `packages/admin/dashboard/src/hooks/use-view-configurations.tsx:36`
- `packages/admin/dashboard/src/components/data-table/data-table.tsx:140`
- `packages/admin/dashboard/src/routes/products/product-list/product-list.tsx:9`
- `packages/admin/dashboard/src/routes/orders/order-list/order-list.tsx:10`
- `packages/admin/dashboard/src/hooks/table/use-table-configuration.tsx:74`

**Answer:** There is no hard-coded default of `true` in the dashboard package. The flag is entirely driven by the server response from `GET /admin/feature-flags` (fetched by `useFeatureFlags`). If that endpoint doesn't return `view_configurations: true` (e.g., not configured, request fails, or is still loading), the code path in `isFeatureEnabled` (`flags[flag] === true`) treats it as disabled. So in a typical dev install it is off unless the backend explicitly returns `true` for `view_configurations` in its feature-flags response — this dashboard package itself does not contain the server-side definition of that endpoint/config (it only consumes it), so I did not find the backend source of truth within `packages/admin/dashboard`.

// @vitest-environment jsdom
import { TooltipProvider } from "@medusajs/ui"
import { cleanup, render, screen } from "@testing-library/react"
import userEvent from "@testing-library/user-event"
import { ReactElement } from "react"
import { afterEach, describe, expect, it } from "vitest"
import { StatusCell } from "./status-cell"

afterEach(() => {
  cleanup()
})

const renderWithTooltipProvider = (ui: ReactElement) => {
  return render(<TooltipProvider delayDuration={0}>{ui}</TooltipProvider>)
}

describe("StatusCell", () => {
  it("renders a short label without a tooltip trigger", () => {
    const { container } = renderWithTooltipProvider(
      <StatusCell color="green">Captured</StatusCell>
    )

    const label = screen.getByText("Captured")
    expect(label).toBeTruthy()
    expect(container.querySelector("[data-state]")).toBeNull()
  })

  it("reveals the full label in a tooltip on hover when the label is long", async () => {
    const user = userEvent.setup()
    renderWithTooltipProvider(
      <StatusCell color="orange">Partially authorized</StatusCell>
    )

    expect(screen.queryByRole("tooltip")).toBeNull()

    const label = screen.getByText("Partially authorized")
    expect(label.getAttribute("data-state")).toBe("closed")

    await user.hover(label)

    const tooltip = await screen.findByRole("tooltip")
    expect(tooltip.textContent).toBe("Partially authorized")
  })
})

All tests pass — 84/84, including the 4 new ones, with no regressions.

## What changed

**Fix** — [status-cell.tsx](packages/admin/dashboard/src/components/table/table-cells/common/status-cell/status-cell.tsx): the shared `StatusCell` component (the one `PaymentStatusCell` renders through) now wraps its truncated `<span>` in the existing `ConditionalTooltip` component, showing a tooltip with the full label whenever it's longer than 10 characters. This is the same pattern `TextCell` already uses elsewhere in the dashboard, just applied here.

Because `StatusCell` is the shared primitive behind every status badge in the admin — payment, fulfillment, product, workflow-execution, category status, etc. — this one change gives all of them the same truncation-tooltip behavior, not just payment status, with no extra code needed per status type.

I deliberately scoped the fix to this component rather than to `PaymentStatusCell` directly, matching what the shared-component architecture already implies: one truncation fix at the shared layer instead of duplicating it per status type.

**Tests added:**
- [status-cell.spec.tsx](packages/admin/dashboard/src/components/table/table-cells/common/status-cell/status-cell.spec.tsx) — unit tests on the shared component: a short label ("Captured") renders with no tooltip trigger at all; a long label ("Partially authorized") is wrapped by the tooltip trigger, and hovering it reveals the full text via `screen.findByRole("tooltip")`.
- [payment-status-cell.spec.tsx](packages/admin/dashboard/src/components/table/table-cells/order/payment-status-cell/payment-status-cell.spec.tsx) — integration-level test on the actual order-table cell, mocking `react-i18next` to return real label strings, covering the exact scenario you asked about: hovering a truncated payment status ("Partially authorized") in the table shows its full text in a tooltip, while a short one ("Captured") shows none.

Both spec files follow this package's existing Vitest/`@testing-library/react`/`user-event` conventions (`.spec.tsx`, `// @vitest-environment jsdom` pragma, `afterEach(cleanup)`), and wrap the component under test in `@medusajs/ui`'s `TooltipProvider` — mirroring how the real app already wraps everything ([providers.tsx](packages/admin/dashboard/src/providers/providers.tsx#L18)) — with `delayDuration={0}` so the hover assertion doesn't need to wait out the real hover delay.

**One thing this doesn't cover:** per my earlier architecture notes, the *configurable* order table (behind the `view_configurations` feature flag, off by default) renders payment status through a separate path — `StatusRenderer` in [cell-renderers.tsx](packages/admin/dashboard/src/lib/table/cell-renderers.tsx#L101-L122) — which calls `@medusajs/ui`'s `StatusBadge` directly, bypassing `StatusCell`. Since that flag is off by default and the fix targets the default order table you're actually using, I left it out; say the word if you also want that path covered.

_**Agent (claude-sonnet-5 2026-09-15 00:10:03Z)**_

Found the real underlying cause — it's a genuine, pre-existing gap in this dev workflow's Vite config, not something new. Vite's top-level `define` only gets applied to client-side source files during a production **build**; for the plain dev server (`vite` with no build), first-party `.ts`/`.tsx` transforms go through a separate esbuild path that ignores `define` entirely and only reads `esbuild.define`. That's confirmed by the fact `__BASE__` — which was already in the config before I touched anything — was *also* never actually substituted in what the dev server serves. Fixing this properly.

_**Agent (claude-sonnet-5 2026-09-15 00:11:18Z)**_

**Root cause:** it wasn't a bug in the tooltip change at all — the standalone `yarn workspace @medusajs/dashboard dev` command had a pre-existing config gap. Vite's top-level `define` (used for `__BASE__`, `__BACKEND_URL__`, etc.) only takes effect during production builds or SSR; the plain dev server transforms `.ts`/`.tsx` files through esbuild directly and ignores `define` entirely, so it's had *zero* effect since before I touched anything — I confirmed `__BASE__` (untouched by any of my edits) was equally unresolved. It just happened to surface as a crash the moment `client.ts` tried to read `__AUTH_TYPE__` early in module evaluation.

**Fix, in [vite.config.mts](packages/admin/dashboard/vite.config.mts):**
- Added the same values under `esbuild: { define: {...} }`, which is the option esbuild's dev-mode file transform actually reads.
- Guarded against esbuild rejecting an actual `undefined` value (it requires every define to be a source-code string, unlike Vite's own `define` handling) by falling back to the literal text `"undefined"` instead of `JSON.stringify(undefined)`.

Verified directly against the running server: `client.ts` now evaluates with `backendUrl = "http://localhost:9000"` and `authType = "session"`, `dashboard-app.tsx`'s `basename` resolves to `"/"`, and the server starts and serves `200` with no errors in the log.

Go to `http://localhost:5173/` again — it should load properly now.

_**Agent (claude-sonnet-5 2026-09-15 00:14:46Z)**_

Here's the exact recipe to recreate it from scratch.

## 1. The actual fix — one file, one change

**File:** [status-cell.tsx](packages/admin/dashboard/src/components/table/table-cells/common/status-cell/status-cell.tsx)

This is the shared component every status badge in the admin (payment, fulfillment, product status, etc.) renders through — `PaymentStatusCell` is a thin wrapper around it. Two edits:

**a) Import the existing `ConditionalTooltip` helper** (already in the codebase, used by `TextCell` for the same truncation problem):
```tsx
import { ConditionalTooltip } from "../../../../common/conditional-tooltip"
```

**b) Wrap the truncated `<span>` in it**, deciding whether to show a tooltip based on label length:
```tsx
export const StatusCell = ({ color, children }: StatusCellProps) => {
  const label = typeof children === "string" ? children : undefined

  return (
    <div className="txt-compact-small text-ui-fg-subtle flex h-full w-full items-center gap-x-2 overflow-hidden">
      {/* ...unchanged colored-dot markup... */}
      <ConditionalTooltip
        content={label}
        showTooltip={!!label && label.length > 10}
      >
        <span className="truncate">{children}</span>
      </ConditionalTooltip>
    </div>
  )
}
```

`ConditionalTooltip` just renders `@medusajs/ui`'s `Tooltip` when `showTooltip` is true, otherwise renders `children` unwrapped — so short statuses ("Captured", "Refunded") get no tooltip at all, while longer ones ("Partially authorized", "Requires action") get one showing the full text on hover. The `> 10` threshold was picked by checking the actual English labels in `getOrderPaymentStatus` — everything ≤10 characters ("Not paid", "Authorized", "Awaiting", "Captured", "Refunded", "Canceled") comfortably fits a normal column; everything longer ("Partially authorized", "Partially refunded", "Partially captured", "Requires action") is the truncation risk.

## 2. The two test files

**[status-cell.spec.tsx](packages/admin/dashboard/src/components/table/table-cells/common/status-cell/status-cell.spec.tsx)** — unit test on the shared component itself, co-located next to it (matching this package's `.spec.tsx` convention):
```tsx
// @vitest-environment jsdom
import { TooltipProvider } from "@medusajs/ui"
import { cleanup, render, screen } from "@testing-library/react"
import userEvent from "@testing-library/user-event"
import { ReactElement } from "react"
import { afterEach, describe, expect, it } from "vitest"
import { StatusCell } from "./status-cell"

afterEach(() => {
  cleanup()
})

const renderWithTooltipProvider = (ui: ReactElement) => {
  return render(<TooltipProvider delayDuration={0}>{ui}</TooltipProvider>)
}

describe("StatusCell", () => {
  it("renders a short label without a tooltip trigger", () => {
    const { container } = renderWithTooltipProvider(
      <StatusCell color="green">Captured</StatusCell>
    )
    const label = screen.getByText("Captured")
    expect(label).toBeTruthy()
    expect(container.querySelector("[data-state]")).toBeNull()
  })

  it("reveals the full label in a tooltip on hover when the label is long", async () => {
    const user = userEvent.setup()
    renderWithTooltipProvider(
      <StatusCell color="orange">Partially authorized</StatusCell>
    )
    expect(screen.queryByRole("tooltip")).toBeNull()
    const label = screen.getByText("Partially authorized")
    expect(label.getAttribute("data-state")).toBe("closed")
    await user.hover(label)
    const tooltip = await screen.findByRole("tooltip")
    expect(tooltip.textContent).toBe("Partially authorized")
  })
})
```

Key details worth understanding if you redo this: Radix's `Tooltip.Trigger` uses `asChild`, so it clones the child element and stamps a `data-state` attribute onto it (`"closed"`, `"delayed-open"`, etc.) — that's how the first test proves *no* tooltip wrapper exists for short labels (no `data-state` at all), without needing jest-dom matchers (this package doesn't wire those up, so plain `.getAttribute()`/`.textContent` checks are used instead of `toHaveAttribute`). Wrapping in `<TooltipProvider delayDuration={0}>` mirrors how the real app wraps everything ([providers.tsx](packages/admin/dashboard/src/providers/providers.tsx#L18)) and makes the hover-to-open transition instant instead of waiting out the real hover delay.

**[payment-status-cell.spec.tsx](packages/admin/dashboard/src/components/table/table-cells/order/payment-status-cell/payment-status-cell.spec.tsx)** — integration test on the real order-table cell, mocking `react-i18next` to return actual English labels instead of raw i18n keys (so the length-based threshold behaves like production):
```tsx

vi.mock("react-i18next", () => ({

      const labels: Record<string, string> = {
        "orders.payment.status.captured": "Captured",
        "orders.payment.status.partiallyAuthorized": "Partially authorized",
      }
      return labels[key] ?? key
    },
  }),
}))

afterEach(() => {
  cleanup()
})

const renderWithTooltipProvider = (ui: ReactElement) => {
  return render(<TooltipProvider delayDuration={0}>{ui}</TooltipProvider>)
}

describe("PaymentStatusCell", () => {
  it("shows a short payment status without a tooltip", () => {
    renderWithTooltipProvider(<PaymentStatusCell status="captured" />)
    expect(screen.getByText("Captured")).toBeTruthy()
    expect(screen.queryByRole("tooltip")).toBeNull()
  })

  it("reveals the full status text on hover when the label is truncated", async () => {

    renderWithTooltipProvider(<PaymentStatusCell status="partially_authorized" />)
    const label = screen.getByText("Partially authorized")
    await user.hover(label)
    const tooltip = await screen.findByRole("tooltip")
    expect(tooltip.textContent).toBe("Partially authorized")
  })
})

117	    PARTIALLY_FULFILLED: "partially_fulfilled",
118	    FULFILLED: "fulfilled",
119	    PARTIALLY_SHIPPED: "partially_shipped",
120	    SHIPPED: "shipped",
121	    DELIVERED: "delivered",
122	    PARTIALLY_DELIVERED: "partially_delivered",
123	    CANCELED: "canceled",
124	  }

126	  let fulfillmentStatus = {}
127	
128	  for (const status in FulfillmentStatus) {
129	    fulfillmentStatus[FulfillmentStatus[status]] = 0

131	
132	  const statusMap = {
133	    canceled_at: FulfillmentStatus.CANCELED,
134	    delivered_at: FulfillmentStatus.DELIVERED,
135	    shipped_at: FulfillmentStatus.SHIPPED,
136	    packed_at: FulfillmentStatus.FULFILLED,

1	import { Modules } from "@medusajs/framework/utils"
2	import {
3	  createWorkflow,
4	  transform,
5	  WorkflowData,
6	  WorkflowResponse,
7	} from "@medusajs/framework/workflows-sdk"
8	import { createPaymentCollectionsStep } from "../../cart"
9	import { createRemoteLinkStep, useQueryGraphStep } from "../../common"
10	
11	/**
12	 * The details of the payment collection to create.
13	 */
14	export type CreateOrderPaymentCollectionWorkflowInput = {
15	  /**
16	   * The id of the order for which to create a payment collection.
17	   */
18	  order_id: string
19	  /**
20	   * The amount of the payment collection.
21	   */
22	  amount: number
23	}
24	
25	export const createOrderPaymentCollectionWorkflowId =
26	  "create-order-payment-collection"
27	/**
28	 * This workflow creates a payment collection for an order. It's used by the
29	 * [Create Payment Collection Admin API Route](https://docs.medusajs.com/api/admin#payment-collections_postpaymentcollections).
30	 *
31	 * You can use this workflow within your customizations or your own custom workflows, allowing you to wrap custom logic around
32	 * creating a payment collection for an order.
33	 *
34	 * @example
35	 * const { result } = await createOrderPaymentCollectionWorkflow(container)
36	 * .run({
37	 *   input: {
38	 *     order_id: "order_123",
39	 *     amount: 10,
40	 *   }
41	 * })
42	 *
43	 * @summary
44	 *
45	 * Create a payment collection for an order.
46	 */
47	export const createOrderPaymentCollectionWorkflow = createWorkflow(
48	  createOrderPaymentCollectionWorkflowId,
49	  (input: WorkflowData<CreateOrderPaymentCollectionWorkflowInput>) => {
50	    const { data: order } = useQueryGraphStep({
51	      entity: "order",
52	      filters: { id: input.order_id },
53	      fields: ["id", "summary", "total", "currency_code", "region_id"],
54	      options: { throwIfKeyNotFound: true, isList: false },
55	    }).config({ name: "get-order" })
56	
57	    const paymentCollectionData = transform(
58	      { order, input },
59	      ({ order, input }) => {
60	        return {
61	          currency_code: order.currency_code,
62	          amount: input.amount,
63	        }
64	      }
65	    )
66	
67	    const createdPaymentCollections = createPaymentCollectionsStep([
68	      paymentCollectionData,
69	    ])
70	
71	    const orderPaymentCollectionLink = transform(
72	      { order, createdPaymentCollections },
73	      ({ order, createdPaymentCollections }) => {
74	        return [
75	          {
76	            [Modules.ORDER]: { order_id: order.id },
77	            [Modules.PAYMENT]: {
78	              payment_collection_id: createdPaymentCollections[0].id,
79	            },
80	          },
81	        ]
82	      }
83	    )
84	
85	    createRemoteLinkStep(orderPaymentCollectionLink).config({
86	      name: "order-payment-collection-link",
87	    })
88	
89	    return new WorkflowResponse(createdPaymentCollections)
90	  }
91	)
92

402	const PaymentBreakdown = ({
403	  order,

405	  refunds,
406	  currencyCode,
407	  plugins,
408	}: {
409	  order: ExtendedOrder
410	  payments: HttpTypes.AdminPayment[]
411	  refunds: ExtendedRefund[]
412	  currencyCode: string
413	  plugins: HttpTypes.AdminPlugin[]
414	}) => {
415	  const pendingAuthSessions = (order.payment_collections ?? []).flatMap((pc) =>
416	    ((pc as any).payment_sessions ?? [])
417	      .filter((s: any) => s.status === "pending_authorization")
418	      .map((s: any) => ({ session_id: s.id }))
419	  )
420	
421	  /**
422	   * Refunds that are not associated with a payment.
423	   */
424	  const orderRefunds = refunds.filter((refund) => refund.payment_id === null)
425	  const creditLines = order.credit_lines ?? []
426	  const creditLineRefunds = creditLines.filter(
427	    (creditLine) => (creditLine.amount as number) < 0
428	  )
429	
430	  const entries = [...orderRefunds, ...payments, ...creditLineRefunds]
431	    .sort((a, b) => {
432	      return (
433	        new Date(a.created_at as string).getTime() -
434	        new Date(b.created_at as string).getTime()
435	      )
436	    })
437	    .map((entry) => {
438	      let type = entry.id.startsWith("pay_") ? "payment" : "refund"
439	
440	      if (entry.id.startsWith("ordcl_")) {
441	        type = "credit_line_refund"
442	      }
443	
444	      return { event: entry, type }
445	    }) as (
446	    | { type: "payment"; event: HttpTypes.AdminPayment }
447	    | { type: "refund"; event: HttpTypes.AdminRefund }
448	    | {
449	        type: "credit_line_refund"
450	        event: OrderCreditLineDTO
451	      }
452	  )[]
453	
454	  return (
455	    <div className="flex flex-col divide-y divide-dashed">
456	      {pendingAuthSessions.map(({ session_id }) => (

461	        />
462	      ))}
463	      {entries.map(({ type, event }) => {
464	        switch (type) {
465	          case "payment":
466	            return (
467	              <Payment
468	                key={event.id}
469	                order={order}
470	                payment={event}
471	                refunds={refunds.filter(
472	                  (refund) => refund.payment_id === event.id
473	                )}
474	                currencyCode={currencyCode}
475	              />
476	            )
477	          case "refund":
478	            return (
479	              <Refund
480	                key={event.id}
481	                refund={event}
482	                currencyCode={currencyCode}
483	              />
484	            )
485	          case "credit_line_refund":
486	            return (
487	              <CreditLine
488	                key={event.id}
489	                creditLine={event}
490	                currencyCode={currencyCode}
491	                plugins={plugins}
492	              />
493	            )
494	        }
495	      })}
496	    </div>
497	  )
498	}
